text: A training company that sells online has to satisfy two very different audiences with one system. Learners want a frictionless shop. The company needs to run an operation: leads, purchase history, invoices, analytics, corporate accounts. Normally that means an e-commerce platform plus a separate CRM, kept in sync - and every sync point is where data drifts. The problem this thesis addresses is to remove that gap entirely.

text: Four families of tools address parts of the problem. Marketplaces like Udemy give you a storefront but you do not own the customer. Moodle manages content, not sales. Salesforce and HubSpot are strong CRMs but know nothing about courses or trainer calendars - and connecting them to a shop reintroduces exactly the integration gap. WooCommerce treats a course as an ordinary product. TrainingIT differs by unifying both sides on one data model.

The goal is not a general-purpose e-commerce platform, nor a general-purpose CRM.

The goal is one coherent product for a training company: a storefront a learner can use without instructions, over a CRM core a small team can actually run - where the AI layer is strictly additive and never a dependency.

text: My contribution is an applied one: a functional system rather than a study. The objectives were a client portal, an administrator portal, a pattern-based event-driven domain layer, an optional AI layer, and persistent storage. The design boundary matters: this is not a general e-commerce platform or a general CRM - it is one coherent product for a training company.

text: The architecture has four layers. The browser runs a Next.js and React client with route guards driven by the local session. It talks to a Spring Boot REST API, which also pushes live catalogue statistics over Server-Sent Events. Behind the controllers is a plain-Java domain layer - commands, services, an event bus and repositories - reached through a single facade. Everything persists to MariaDB over JDBC with HikariCP.

text: The domain layer is deliberately organised around the Gang-of-Four patterns. A facade gives the controllers one entry point. Every write is a command. Lead scoring is a strategy, chosen per contact type. Factories build notifications and activities, builders assemble contacts and opportunities. The most important one is Observer: the event bus is what turns a single click into several automatic reactions.

text: This is the core data model. Because both portals are served by the same back end, there is one schema rather than two. Note two design decisions: a review has no table of its own - the rating and feedback live directly on the enrolment, which guarantees one review per learner per course and means only a buyer can review. And a session invoice is generated from a meditation session, never entered by hand.

text: This sequence is the central idea of the solution. The client confirms a purchase; the facade finds or creates the contact and the course session, saves the enrolment, and publishes an EnrollmentCreatedEvent. The observers react on their own. Meanwhile the statistics broadcaster pushes the changed figures to every subscribed browser, so the learner count on the home page moves without a reload. The review at the bottom is validated against a prior purchase before it is stored on the enrolment.

text: The AI layer was the part I extended furthest myself. There are four features, all sharing one Claude client and one API key: a chatbot grounded in the live catalogue, a recommendation quiz for visitors, per-company recommendations for corporate training, and live page translation. I wrote the prompts, the endpoints, the structured JSON handling and the interfaces. The important property is that the layer is strictly additive - remove the key and the buttons simply do not render.

text: Because correctness here depends on a user action propagating through the whole system, testing concentrated on three things. Input validation on both client and server, including a chain-of-responsibility validator for contacts. Robustness properties I verified by forcing the failure: idempotent invoices, isolated observer failures, graceful AI degradation, guarded deletions. And functional verification of the end-to-end journeys against a real database. The Spring Boot test harness is in place as a foundation for an automated suite, which I list as future work.

text: To conclude. TrainingIT delivers a client portal, a seven-tab administrator portal, a pattern-based event-driven domain layer, live statistics and reporting, and an optional AI layer - meeting the objectives set out in the introduction. The limitations are honest ones: the test suite is a foundation rather than full coverage, and authentication would need hardening for production. The central result is that the storefront and the CRM are not two integrated systems but one. Thank you - I am happy to take questions.
